cards.front: What sets the oxygen content of the blood leaving the lung?
cards.back: It is a flow-weighted mix of the oxygen content from every lung unit, and each unit's content is set by its own ventilation-perfusion ratio.
cards.quote: blood leaving the lung is a flow-weighted mix of the oxygen content from every unit, and each unit's content is set by its own ratio of ventilation to perfusion

cards.front: Why does raising a lung unit's ventilation-perfusion ratio above about 1 add almost no oxygen content to its blood?
cards.back: Its PO2 cannot climb past the inspired 150 mmHg, and hemoglobin is already about 98% saturated.
cards.why: Lowering a ratio below about 0.5, by contrast, removes a lot of content.
cards.quote: its PO2 cannot climb past the inspired 150 mmHg, and hemoglobin is already about 98% saturated

cards.front: A lung unit that is perfused but not ventilated has a ventilation-perfusion ratio of zero and is called a {{c1::shunt}}.
cards.quote: At a ratio of zero the unit is a shunt: perfused and not ventilated.
cards.section: One ratio sets each unit's gas

cards.front: A lung unit that is ventilated but not perfused has an infinite ventilation-perfusion ratio and is called {{c1::dead space}}.
cards.quote: At an infinite ratio it is dead space: ventilated and not perfused.
cards.section: One ratio sets each unit's gas

cards.front: At rest, what are the typical PO2 and PCO2 of mixed venous blood arriving at the lung?
cards.back: PO2 about 40 mmHg and PCO2 about 46 mmHg.
cards.quote: At rest its PO2 is typically about 40 mmHg and its PCO2 about 46 mmHg.
cards.section: One ratio sets each unit's gas

cards.front: What PO2 and PCO2 does blood leaving a shunt unit carry, and what gas sits in a dead-space unit?
cards.back: Shunt blood leaves as mixed venous blood (PO2 about 40, PCO2 about 46 mmHg). The dead-space unit holds inspired gas: PO2 about 150 mmHg, PCO2 near zero.
cards.why: Shunt blood never meets fresh air; dead-space gas never meets blood.
cards.quote: Shunt blood never meets fresh air, so it leaves as mixed venous blood, PO2 about 40 and PCO2 about 46 mmHg
cards.section: One ratio sets each unit's gas

cards.front: A resting lung has 4.2 L per min of alveolar ventilation and 5 L per min of blood flow. What is its overall ventilation-perfusion ratio?
cards.back: 4.2 / 5 = 0.84, the evenly matched ratio of a resting lung.
cards.quote: 0.84 is the evenly matched ratio of a resting lung, 4.2 L of air over 5 L of blood per min
cards.section: One ratio sets each unit's gas

cards.front: As a lung unit's ventilation-perfusion ratio rises above the matched value, how do its PO2 and PCO2 change?
cards.back: PO2 climbs with diminishing returns and never passes the inspired 150 mmHg; PCO2 falls toward zero.
cards.quote: Upward it climbs with diminishing returns and never passes the inspired 150. PCO2 runs the other way.
cards.section: One ratio sets each unit's gas

cards.front: What is the commonest cause of low arterial oxygen?
cards.back: Ventilation-perfusion mismatch; with shunt it is among the most frequent.
cards.quote: Ventilation-perfusion mismatch is the commonest cause of low arterial oxygen, and the next two sections show why.
cards.section: One ratio sets each unit's gas

cards.front: By Henry's law, about {{c1::0.003}} mL of oxygen dissolves per dL of blood per mmHg of PO2.
cards.quote: About 0.003 mL of oxygen dissolves per dL of blood per mmHg
cards.section: Partial pressure is not content

cards.front: A patient breathing oxygen has an arterial PO2 of 600 mmHg. Using Henry's law (0.003 mL O2 per dL per mmHg), how much oxygen is dissolved per dL of blood, and how does that compare with the amount at 100 mmHg?
cards.back: 0.003 × 600 = 1.8 mL per dL, against 0.3 mL per dL at 100 mmHg. Both are small next to the roughly 20 mL per dL carried by hemoglobin.
cards.quote: so 100 mmHg dissolves only 0.3 mL per dL, which is why nearly all of it rides on hemoglobin
cards.section: Partial pressure is not content

cards.front: In a simple one-unit lung model, raising the ventilation-perfusion ratio from 0.84 to 10 raises PO2 by about 44 mmHg. Why does oxygen content rise only from 20.0 to 20.4 mL per dL?
cards.back: The unit is on the flat top of the dissociation curve: hemoglobin is already about 98% saturated, so extra PO2 adds little content.
cards.quote: On the flat top, ratios from 0.84 up to 10 raise PO2 by some 44 mmHg but content only from 20.0 to 20.4 mL per dL
cards.section: Partial pressure is not content

cards.front: Two lung units receive equal blood flow. Unit A leaves blood at PO2 45 mmHg with 16.4 mL O2 per dL; unit B at PO2 122 mmHg with 20.2 mL O2 per dL. What is the mixed arterial content, and why is arterial PO2 about 59 mmHg rather than 84?
cards.back: (16.4 + 20.2) / 2 = 18.3 mL per dL, about 90% saturation, which reads off the curve at about 59 mmHg. 84 is the average of the pressures, but blood mixes oxygen content, not partial pressure.
cards.quote: Blood does not mix partial pressures; it mixes oxygen.
cards.section: Two units: why a spread costs oxygen

cards.front: In a two-unit lung with one low-ratio and one high-ratio unit, why can the high-ratio unit not make up for the low-ratio one?
cards.back: Extra air raises the high-ratio unit's PO2 on the flat top of the curve, adding little content, while the low-ratio unit falls onto the steep part and loses a lot.
cards.quote: Nearly twice its share of air raised its PO2 by more than 20 mmHg but added only 0.2 mL per dL: the flat top.
cards.section: Two units: why a spread costs oxygen

cards.front: Why does arterial PCO2 hardly change when a spread of ventilation-perfusion ratios lowers arterial PO2?
cards.back: The carbon dioxide curve is nearly straight, so mixing contents is close to mixing partial pressures, and the extra carbon dioxide high-ratio units blow off offsets most of what low-ratio units keep, so PCO2 hardly moves at first.
cards.why: Any small shortfall in carbon dioxide output is made up when the controller raises total ventilation.
cards.quote: Carbon dioxide's curve is nearly straight, so mixing contents is close to mixing partial pressures
cards.section: Two units: why a spread costs oxygen

cards.front: A person with ventilation-perfusion mismatch breathes harder. What happens to arterial PCO2 and arterial PO2, and why?
cards.back: Arterial PCO2 falls, but arterial PO2 improves much less. The extra air mostly reaches open units, which shed more carbon dioxide but are already on the flat top for oxygen.
cards.quote: The extra air mostly reaches the open units, which can shed more carbon dioxide but load little more oxygen.
cards.section: Two units: why a spread costs oxygen

cards.front: Can a wide alveolar-arterial oxygen difference arise with no diffusion limitation and no shunt?
cards.back: Yes. A spread of ventilation-perfusion ratios alone is enough, because blood mixes by oxygen content and the dissociation curve is flat at the top.
cards.quote: That gap, the alveolar-arterial oxygen difference, appeared with no diffusion limit and no shunt: a spread of ratios is enough.
cards.section: Two units: why a spread costs oxygen

cards.front: In the alveolar gas equation, PAO2 = FiO2 × (PB − 47) − PaCO2 / R, R is the {{c1::respiratory quotient}}, about 0.8 at steady state on a mixed diet.
cards.back: Carbon dioxide produced per oxygen consumed.
cards.quote: the respiratory quotient: carbon dioxide produced per oxygen consumed, about 0.8 at steady state on a mixed diet.
cards.section: Measuring the gap: alveolar PO2 and the A-a difference

cards.front: Name the assumptions built into the simplified alveolar gas equation.
cards.back: A steady state; an assumed rather than measured R (about 0.8); an inspired oxygen fraction near that of air; and arterial PCO2 standing in for alveolar PCO2.
cards.quote: a value for R assumed rather than measured, an inspired oxygen fraction near that of air, and arterial PCO2 standing in for alveolar PCO2
cards.section: Measuring the gap: alveolar PO2 and the A-a difference

cards.front: A young adult breathing air at sea level (PB 760 mmHg, water vapour 47 mmHg, R 0.8) has PaCO2 30 mmHg and PaO2 90 mmHg. Calculate PAO2 and the alveolar-arterial oxygen difference. Is it normal?
cards.back: PAO2 = 0.21 × 713 − 30 / 0.8 = 149.7 − 37.5 = 112.2 mmHg. A-a difference = 112.2 − 90 = 22.2 mmHg: widened, since a young adult's is under about 10 mmHg.
cards.quote: The alveolar-arterial oxygen difference is PAO2 minus PaO2. It is under about 10 mmHg in a young adult
cards.section: Measuring the gap: alveolar PO2 and the A-a difference

cards.front: Explain the mass-balance logic that lets mixed expired PCO2 reveal the dead-space fraction of a breath.
cards.back: All expired carbon dioxide comes from units that exchanged; dead-space gas adds none. So mixed expired PCO2 is the alveolar value diluted by dead-space gas, and the degree of dilution gives the dead-space fraction.
cards.quote: All the carbon dioxide in an expired breath came from units that exchanged, and dead-space gas contributes none
cards.section: Dead space: the high end, measured

cards.front: A resting adult has PaCO2 45 mmHg, mixed expired PECO2 30 mmHg, tidal volume 600 mL and rate 10 per min. Find the physiologic dead-space fraction, dead-space volume and alveolar ventilation.
cards.back: VD/VT = (45 − 30) / 45 = 15/45 = 1/3 (about 0.33). VD = 200 mL. Alveolar ventilation = (600 − 200) × 10 = 4,000 mL per min.
cards.why: Bohr mass balance in Enghoff's arterial form, assuming arterial PCO2 equals mean alveolar PCO2 (no shunt).
cards.quote: VD/VT = (PaCO2 - PECO2) / PaCO2
cards.section: Dead space: the high end, measured

cards.front: How does physiologic dead space (from the Bohr-Enghoff calculation) differ from what Fowler's single-breath nitrogen method measures?
cards.back: Physiologic dead space includes alveolar units ventilated far more than they are perfused. Fowler's method measures something closer to the anatomic dead space of the conducting airways. They are not interchangeable.
cards.quote: measures something closer to the anatomic dead space of the conducting airways; the two are not interchangeable
cards.section: Dead space: the high end, measured

cards.front: Some blood reaches the left heart without being ventilated (a shunt). What happens to the dead-space fraction calculated as (PaCO2 − PECO2) / PaCO2, and why?
cards.back: It is inflated. Shunted blood raises PaCO2 above mean alveolar PCO2, breaking the assumption that arterial PCO2 equals alveolar PCO2.
cards.quote: because that blood raises PaCO2 above PACO2 and inflates the computed fraction
cards.section: Dead space: the high end, measured

cards.front: Why does a raised dead-space fraction usually not raise arterial PCO2?
cards.back: The respiratory controller raises total ventilation to defend PCO2, so the cost appears as more work of breathing.
cards.quote: the controller raises total ventilation to defend it (control of breathing), so the cost appears as more work of breathing
cards.section: Dead space: the high end, measured

cards.front: Low oxygen dilates systemic arterioles. What does it do to pulmonary arterioles, and what does that achieve?
cards.back: It constricts them, so blood flow leaves a poorly ventilated region instead of pooling in it, pushing that unit's ventilation-perfusion ratio back up.
cards.quote: The pulmonary circulation does the opposite, so flow leaves a poorly ventilated region rather than pooling in it.
cards.section: Hypoxic lungs constrict their own arteries

cards.front: In an anaesthetized, pump-ventilated cat, ventilation with 10.5 percent oxygen strongly raised pulmonary arterial pressure, and the rise survived cutting the vagi and removing the stellate ganglia. What does this show, and what can it not show?
cards.back: Hypoxia constricts lung vessels, at least in part by a direct action rather than through those nerves. It cannot prove a resistance change without flow and outflow pressure, nor test regional matching, because the whole lung was hypoxic.
cards.quote: the rise survived cutting the vagi and removing the stellate ganglia
cards.section: Hypoxic lungs constrict their own arteries

cards.front: In pulmonary artery smooth muscle, hypoxia inhibits an outward {{c1::potassium}} current, depolarizing the cell and opening voltage-gated calcium channels.
cards.back: One route among several, including mitochondrial reactive oxygen species and calcium sensitization.
cards.quote: hypoxia inhibits an outward potassium current in pulmonary artery smooth muscle, depolarizing the cell and opening voltage-gated calcium channels
cards.section: Hypoxic lungs constrict their own arteries

cards.front: A lung has some poorly ventilated units, and a drug blunts hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction. What happens to arterial PO2, and why?
cards.back: It falls further. Flow returns to the poorly ventilated units, so a larger share of the blood leaves with low oxygen content, and the mix drops.
cards.quote: Flow returns to the poorly ventilated units, so a larger share of the blood leaves with low content, and the mix drops.
cards.section: Hypoxic lungs constrict their own arteries

cards.front: A rise in pulmonary arterial pressure during hypoxia could reflect more flow or higher downstream pressure rather than vasoconstriction. Design a preparation in which a pressure rise can only mean a resistance rise.
cards.back: Use an isolated lung, pump-ventilated and perfused at constant flow with a set outflow pressure. Resistance = (inflow − outflow pressure) / flow, so with flow and outflow fixed, a rise in inflow pressure is a rise in resistance; extrinsic nerves and hormones are also removed.
cards.why: Add time controls and a potassium chloride contraction control.
cards.quote: Then resistance = (inflow pressure - outflow pressure) / flow, so a pressure rise can only be a resistance rise
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: Isolated, buffer-perfused lungs from mice lacking Cox4i2 show no acute constriction to hypoxia but constrict normally to potassium chloride. What does this place, and what does the potassium chloride control not test?
cards.back: It places the defect in sensing or its signaling, upstream of contraction, in mouse lungs. Potassium chloride depolarizes the cell directly, so it shows the contractile machinery works but does not test the potassium-channel step.
cards.quote: showed no acute constriction to hypoxia while constricting normally to potassium chloride
cards.section: The Cox4i2 knockout and the sensor

cards.front: In the upright human lung, why is the ventilation-perfusion ratio higher at the apex than at the base?
cards.back: Both ventilation and perfusion per unit volume are greater at the base, but perfusion changes more steeply from apex to base.
cards.quote: both ventilation and perfusion per unit volume are greater at the base than at the apex, and perfusion changes more steeply
cards.section: Top and bottom of the upright lung

cards.front: In a region of lung, alveolar pressure comes to exceed both pulmonary arterial and venous pressure. Which West zone is this, what is its blood flow, and how does that region behave for gas exchange?
cards.back: Zone 1 (alveolar > arterial > venous): no blood flow. Still ventilated, the region acts as dead space, with an infinite ratio.
cards.why: Zones are pressure relations, not anatomic bands, so posture, blood volume and ventilation can move them.
cards.quote: They state a condition for flow rather than mark anatomic bands
cards.section: Top and bottom of the upright lung

cards.front: Which three measurements separate most mechanisms of low arterial PO2?
cards.back: Arterial PCO2, the alveolar-arterial oxygen difference, and the response of arterial PO2 to a higher inspired oxygen fraction.
cards.quote: arterial PCO2, the alveolar-arterial difference, and the response to a higher inspired oxygen fraction
cards.section: Sorting low arterial oxygen with three numbers

cards.front: A patient breathing air at sea level (PB 760, water vapour 47 mmHg, R 0.8) has PaCO2 60 mmHg and PaO2 50 mmHg. Is hypoventilation alone enough to explain the low PaO2?
cards.back: No. PAO2 = 149.7 − 60 / 0.8 = 149.7 − 75 = 74.7 mmHg, so the A-a difference is 24.7 mmHg, widened. Hypoventilation alone keeps the difference normal, so another mechanism (mismatch, shunt or diffusion limitation) is also present.
cards.quote: Low PO2, high PCO2, normal difference: hypoventilation, since mismatch, shunt and diffusion limitation all widen the difference.
cards.section: Sorting low arterial oxygen with three numbers

cards.front: A resting adult has PaCO2 40 mmHg at an alveolar ventilation of 4.2 L per min. Alveolar ventilation falls to 3.5 L per min with carbon dioxide output unchanged. What is the new PaCO2?
cards.back: PaCO2 is inversely proportional to alveolar ventilation at fixed carbon dioxide output: 40 × 4.2 / 3.5 = 48 mmHg.
cards.quote: Halve alveolar ventilation to 2.1 L per min at unchanged carbon dioxide output
cards.section: Sorting low arterial oxygen with three numbers

cards.front: Two patients both have a wide A-a difference and normal PaCO2 on air. On pure oxygen, patient 1's PaO2 rises far above 500 mmHg; patient 2's reaches only about 220 mmHg. Which mechanism fits each?
cards.back: Patient 1: oxygen-responsive hypoxemia, fits ventilation-perfusion mismatch (low-ratio units are still ventilated, so oxygen reaches them; diffusion limitation looks alike and needs further measurements). Patient 2: shunt; shunted blood never sees the oxygen and dilutes what the rest achieves.
cards.quote: The shunted blood never saw the oxygen, and it dilutes whatever the rest achieves.
cards.section: Sorting low arterial oxygen with three numbers

cards.front: On air, end-capillary content in ventilated units is 20.00 mL O2 per dL and mixed venous content is 15.20 mL O2 per dL. If one tenth of the flow bypasses ventilated units, what is arterial oxygen content?
cards.quote: Take the illustrative contents from oxygen transport: hemoglobin 15 g per dL, end-capillary content on air 20.00 mL O2 per dL, mixed venous 15.20.
cards.section: Sorting low arterial oxygen with three numbers

cards.front: End-capillary oxygen content is 20.00 mL per dL, arterial content 19.28 mL per dL and mixed venous content 15.20 mL per dL. What fraction of the flow is shunt?
cards.why: Arterial shortfall over the largest possible shortfall.
cards.quote: as the arterial shortfall over the largest possible shortfall (end-capillary minus arterial, over end-capillary minus mixed venous)
cards.section: Sorting low arterial oxygen with three numbers

cards.front: Why does supplemental oxygen usually raise arterial PO2 well in ventilation-perfusion mismatch, and when is the correction incomplete?
cards.back: Low-ratio units are still ventilated, so filling them with oxygen usually saturates their blood. At very low ratios the correction is incomplete, and high oxygen can collapse the unit by absorption atelectasis.
cards.quote: A low-ratio unit is still ventilated, so filling it with oxygen usually saturates its blood
cards.section: Sorting low arterial oxygen with three numbers

cards.front: At rest, about how long does a red cell spend in a pulmonary capillary, and about how long does oxygen equilibration take?
cards.back: About 0.75 s in the capillary; roughly 0.25 s suffices. So oxygen transfer in healthy lungs at rest is limited by blood flow, not by the barrier.
cards.quote: A red cell spends about 0.75 s in a pulmonary capillary at rest and roughly 0.25 s suffices for equilibration
cards.section: Sorting low arterial oxygen with three numbers

cards.front: During heavy exercise, cardiac output rises and capillary transit time shortens. Predict how this can affect oxygen equilibration and the A-a difference in a healthy person.
cards.back: If transit falls toward the roughly 0.25 s needed, blood can leave before it equilibrates: oxygen becomes diffusion limited and the A-a difference widens.
cards.why: Rests on the 0.75 s versus 0.25 s margin and on diffusion limitation widening the difference.
cards.quote: though oxygen can become diffusion limited when transit is shortened
cards.section: Sorting low arterial oxygen with three numbers

cards.front: Airways narrow in some lung regions but not others. Predict arterial PO2, arterial PCO2 (after the controller responds), the A-a difference, and the response to 40 percent oxygen.
cards.back: Arterial PO2 falls and the A-a difference widens; arterial PCO2 stays near normal because total ventilation rises; arterial PO2 rises well on extra oxygen.
cards.why: Content mixing on the flat-topped curve; a near-straight carbon dioxide curve; low-ratio units are still ventilated.
cards.quote: widen the spread, as when airways narrow in some regions and not others, and the same arithmetic produces a large one
cards.section: Two units: why a spread costs oxygen

cards.front: A hypoventilating patient has PaCO2 80 mmHg and an A-a difference of about 8 mmHg. She is given FiO2 0.30 at sea level (PB 760, water vapour 47 mmHg, R 0.8) with ventilation unchanged. Estimate PaO2 and PaCO2. What does extra oxygen fix?
cards.back: PAO2 = 0.30 × 713 − 80 / 0.8 = 213.9 − 100 = 113.9 mmHg, so PaO2 is about 106 mmHg, but PaCO2 stays at 80 mmHg. Oxygen corrects the hypoxemia, not the carbon dioxide retention.
cards.why: Simplified alveolar gas equation; PaCO2 depends on alveolar ventilation and carbon dioxide output, not FiO2.
cards.quote: while PaCO2 stays at 80 mmHg
cards.section: Sorting low arterial oxygen with three numbers

cards.front: A whole animal breathes a low-oxygen mixture, as at altitude, so every lung region is equally hypoxic. Predict pulmonary arterial pressure, and whether hypoxic vasoconstriction improves matching.
cards.back: Pulmonary arterial pressure rises, as in the cat ventilated with 10.5 percent oxygen. With every region equally hypoxic, constriction is global, so it cannot steer flow toward better-ventilated units.
cards.why: Regional benefit needs a regional difference in ventilation.
cards.quote: Ventilation with 10.5 percent oxygen strongly raised the pressure and pure oxygen lowered it slightly
cards.section: Hypoxic lungs constrict their own arteries
